{"id": "44:47/q07", "question": "What action does 'faʿtilūhu' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the root is glossed as dragging, pushing, simple leading, or breaking like firewood; al-Ālūsī objects to the last as needing syntactic supplementation.", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q07/p1", "position": "Drag or drive him away by force, roughly and with humiliation.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutaybah compares forcibly bringing someone before a ruler; al-Layth describes taking a man's lapel and pulling him toward prison or calamity, or leading a camel by its reins. Ibn al-Sikkīt cites عتلته/أعتلته to prison and also عتنته for violent pushing. Al-Farazdaq's تعتل line, and another line likening the dragged man to a large slaughter camel, witness the force. Al-Qurṭubī adds a horse poem; al-Rāghib says gripping a garment is an example, not essential to the sense. Al-Biqāʿī quotes al-Rāzī's grip on the gathered chest garment and adds speed and helplessness; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah likens it to leading criminals. Bursawī cites Tāj al-Maṣādir and al-Qāmūs, the latter also defining مُعْتَل as one strong enough to drag. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn connect the root to an uncouth, coarse person. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr mention dragging from behind; Mujāhid is reported by al-Ṭabrisī as dragging him on his face. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes forceful shaking."}, {"id": "44:47/q07/p2", "position": "Push or shove him violently, in some reports face-down.", "reasons": "Mujāhid glosses the verb as pushing; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says take and push him into Hell's middle. Muqātil and Mujāhid are reported as pushing him face-down; Muqātil specifies Abū Jahl and Hell's sixth gate. Ibn al-Sikkīt says عتلته and عتنته both denote violent pushing. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes pushing among the verb's senses; Ibn Kathīr describes shoving him from behind."}, {"id": "44:47/q07/p3", "position": "Lead him along toward Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī's short gloss says 'lead him along'; al-Wāḥidī reports him specifying the destination as Hell's middle and connecting it with 37:55. The gloss does not itself spell out the violence other sources give."}, {"id": "44:47/q07/p4", "position": "Break, crush, or wrench him as one does firewood.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes the firewood comparison to al-Aʿmash; al-Durr gives it from Mujāhid. Al-Ālūsī reports it from both and says that this sense requires an implied element or attaching the prepositional phrase to 'take him'; he favors the familiar dragging sense."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q08", "question": "Which commands does 'to the middle of Hell' modify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q08/p1", "position": "It attaches to both 'take him' and 'drag him.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says both verbs imply driving the sinner forcefully to that destination."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q09", "question": "What is 'sawāʾ al-jaḥīm,' the destination?", "turns_on": "Whether 'sawāʾ' emphasizes the center, the principal area reached by heat from every side, or its broader lexical senses.", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q09/p1", "position": "The middle or center of Hellfire.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are cited for the center. Al-Ṭabrisī, Bursawī and al-Ālūsī explain 'sawāʾ' by equal distance from every edge. Al-Kalbī links the middle with 37:55; Ibn al-Jawzī also cites 37:55 for 'sawāʾ.' Al-Nasafī and Bursawī call it the greatest or principal part as well. Al-Biqāʿī calls 'jaḥīm' the fiercely blazing Fire and the place where the sinner's food tree grows; Muqātil names its sixth gate. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says its central position lets Hell envelop him, linked by him to 29:54. Iṣlāḥī calls it Hell's depth."}, {"id": "44:47/q09/p2", "position": "Hell's main part, where heat reaches the sinner from every side.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as al-Ḥasan's alternative to the gloss 'middle'; al-Nasafī and Bursawī also call the central place its greatest or principal part."}, {"id": "44:47/q09/p3", "position": "The word sawāʾ can also mean justice or evenness.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives these lexical senses alongside the middle sense; he does not explicitly replace the verse's destination with an abstract quality."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q10", "question": "What report describes the number of guards at the seizure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q10/p1", "position": "Seventy thousand keepers rush toward the condemned person when God orders his seizure.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits this as a report without a named transmitter in the note."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q11", "question": "How does this scene relate to other Quranic passages?", "turns_on": "These are different textual connections rather than competing explanations.", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q11/p1", "position": "37:55 gives a related glimpse of someone in Hell's middle.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits al-Kalbī's comparison when specifying the sinner's destination; Ibn al-Jawzī also cites 37:55 for 'sawāʾ' as center."}, {"id": "44:47/q11/p2", "position": "29:54 supports the image of Hell enveloping the sinner.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links the central destination in 44:47 to the statement that Hell surrounds the unbelievers."}, {"id": "44:47/q11/p3", "position": "52:13 likewise describes disbelievers violently thrust into Hell on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites that passage as a parallel to the violent movement here."}, {"id": "44:47/q11/p4", "position": "96:17–18 identifies the guards as the zabāniyah.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites these verses when naming the angels addressed by God's order."}, {"id": "44:47/q11/p5", "position": "The tormenting food tree mentioned nearby is also connected with 37:62.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says the zaqqūm tree of verse 43 grows in Hell for punishment and cites 37:62; al-Biqāʿī identifies the fiercely blazing Fire here as the place from which the sinner's food tree emerges."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q12", "question": "How does the following boiling-water description intensify this scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q12/p1", "position": "It speaks of pouring torment from boiling water, strengthening the image beyond simply pouring water on the head.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares the expected wording about pouring water from above and calls the actual wording a stronger metaphor, citing 2:250. Iṣlāḥī describes the wardens continuing from seizure and dragging to pouring boiling water over the sinner's head."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q13", "question": "How does this punishment fit the surrounding account of judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q13/p1", "position": "It depicts the disbelievers' fate after arguments for resurrection and just reward and punishment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the passage first offers intellectual, historical and natural evidence, then contrasts believers' and disbelievers' fates; he identifies denial of afterlife as the source of Quraysh rebellion and disregard for the future. Kur'an Yolu says afterlife realities are described through worldly perceptions, desires and fears; Judgment Day separates and repays good and evil, innocent and guilty, oppressed and oppressor, and those destined for Paradise and Hell."}]}
{"id": "44:47/q14", "question": "What inward torment does the scene signify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:47/q14/p1", "position": "Regret, deprivation, and the burning ache of separation within the fires.", "reasons": "Bursawī adds this spiritual significance to the physical scene."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q01", "question": "What does the command to taste convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the command is explained by its object, its humiliating force, or Bursevī's account of newly perceived prior pain.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q01/p1", "position": "Experience the punishment of Hell.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it torment; al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Bursevī and the Study Quran say punishment. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls tasting a metaphor for experiencing; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it conveys full perception of pain and pleasure. The Study Quran links other punishment-as-tasting verses (3:106, 3:181, 4:56, 6:30, 7:39, 8:35, 8:50, 10:52, 22:22, 32:14, 32:20, 34:42, 46:34). Ṭabrisī reports Muqātil's scene: the keeper lifts the sinner over the fire, his head parts from his brain, and extremely hot water is poured in; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the address occurs amid successive punishments. Iṣlāḥī says they taste the torment they had questioned."}, {"id": "44:49/q01/p2", "position": "The imperative insults, threatens, and humiliates the condemned.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it mockery and humiliation; Bursevī says the punishment is degrading; Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies a humiliating imperative. Al-Burhān calls it denial and rebuke, and al-Biqāʿī says it recalls the messengers' worldly warning of the sinner's lowliness. Al-Itqān lists threat, insult, humiliation through transformation, and challenge exposing inability among imperative functions; it also uses this verse as sarcastic address."}, {"id": "44:49/q01/p3", "position": "He begins to feel the pain of injustice that he failed to sense during life.", "reasons": "Bursevī says heedlessness and veiling numbed him to punishment already present in this world; death awakens perception of it."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q02", "question": "Who speaks the taunt?", "turns_on": "Whether the utterance has an identified divine or angelic speaker, is implicit quoted speech, or is the situation expressed as speech.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q02/p1", "position": "An angel or the guardians of Hell speak it.", "reasons": "Muqātil names the keeper; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Iṣlāḥī and the Study Quran identify an angel or wardens. The Study Quran says they execute God's command."}, {"id": "44:49/q02/p2", "position": "God directly addresses the disbelievers.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports this interpretation."}, {"id": "44:49/q02/p3", "position": "The situation and punishment themselves ex

press the taunt, with no identified speaker.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī reports this reading as an alternative to speech by the wardens."}, {"id": "44:49/q02/p4", "position": "It is a quoted utterance introduced by an omitted verb of saying, with the speaker left implicit.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies an ellipsis such as 'say to him' or 'it is said to him'."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q03", "question": "How is إِنَّكَ read and construed?", "turns_on": "The vowel on the hamza determines an independent assertion and pause or a subordinate causal construction; commentators note their meanings can converge.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q03/p1", "position": "Most readers use kasra, innaka, as a new independent clause: 'indeed you are'.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Samīn, Ibn al-Jazarī's Nashr and Ibn ʿĀshūr contrast it with al-Kisāʾī's fatḥa. Al-Naḥḥās says the clause begins a sentence and prefers the supported majority reading; al-Qurṭubī says one pauses after 'taste'. Al-Fārisī and Abū ʿAlī (via Ibn al-Jawzī) say the independent assertion echoes Abū Jahl's own claim; al-Samīn says it still conveys a cause. The Study Quran renders it 'surely you'."}, {"id": "44:49/q03/p2", "position": "Al-Kisāʾī reads fatḥa, annaka, making the clause causal: 'because you are'; other witnesses also transmit it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn, al-Nashr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Qiraat-ER note the variant. Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Ḥasan from ʿAlī; al-Ālūsī names al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. Al-Fārisī expands it as 'taste because you are'; al-Bayḍāwī also allows attachment to an omitted 'punishment'; Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies an implied lām of purpose, and Qiraat-ER notes a subordinating or object-like link. Al-Qurṭubī says no pause after 'taste'. Al-Biqāʿī says speech and enacted punishment meet the sinner's former self-praise; the Study Quran links doubt to haughtiness. Al-Naḥḥās objects that this boast is less than the disbelief the construction would imply."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q04", "question": "What does the detached pronoun أَنتَ do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q04/p1", "position": "It singles out and emphatically reinforces the addressee.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says it isolates the supposedly mighty sinner against those who exposed his worthlessness. Ibn ʿĀshūr says a detached nominative emphasizes the attached pronoun in innaka and that such emphasis requires this nominative form; he says the emphasis heightens sarcasm."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q05", "question": "What does ٱلْعَزِيزُ denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q05/p1", "position": "A mighty, powerful, protected person who prevails.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Dāmghānī give 'impregnable' or mighty; al-Dāmghānī cites parallel descriptions of strength in 4:158, 48:7, 63:8, 4:139 and 35:10. Al-Biqāʿī specifies one who overcomes and is never overcome. The Abu Jahl reports frame it as power and protection in Mecca's valley."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q06", "question": "What does ٱلْكَرِيمُ denote here?", "turns_on": "Whether karīm describes the usual honorable trait or the condemned man's inflated self-description.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q06/p1", "position": "Noble or generous, with dignity and proud self-regard.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī combines generosity, dignity of soul and proud refusal. The reports of Abū Jahl's boast use nobility, honor or generosity as near wordings; al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz has 'generous'."}, {"id": "44:49/q06/p2", "position": "Self-honoring, arrogant or noble only in one's own estimation.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives conceited or self-honoring; al-Dāmghānī says it is the condemned man's own claim. Ibn al-Jawzī's Nuzha reports an exegetical sense 'arrogant' or 'self-important', used mockingly; Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās give 'in his own eyes'."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q07", "question": "Why is the condemned called 'the mighty, the noble'?", "turns_on": "Whether the titles repeat the sinner's self-praise, invert their surface meaning, or acknowledge real but useless social status.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q07/p1", "position": "The titles throw his former boast or self-image back at him in scorn.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Majāz, Qatāda and many later commentators say Abū Jahl styled himself the mightiest and noblest in Mecca; the keepers repeat his claim. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and Abū ʿAlī say the titles are true only in his own eyes or claim. Al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī cite Zahrat al-Yaman's self-praise and Jarīr's retort; al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī compare the alleged partners in 28:62. Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm compares the unbelievers' mocking address in 15:6. Al-Samīn also cites Jarīr. Al-Biqāʿī says repeating what the sinner and followers believed compounds the rebuke; al-Burhān calls it taḥakkum and speech framed by the addressee's belief. Ṭabāṭabāʾī recalls his expected good standing with God (41:50); the Study Quran says the speech ridicules worldly self-image. Al-Fārisī says the seeming praise can be understood as 'according to you': Arabic may voice someone's claim with that qualification left implicit, as in sarcastic and hostile forms of address; it does not affirm the claimed status or alleged idols."}, {"id": "44:49/q07/p2", "position": "The apparent praise is sarcastic reversal: he is now lowly, weak and humiliated.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba records the opposite-sense gloss; Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's 'neither mighty nor noble'; Qatāda and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr similarly negate the titles and stress insult. Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Burhān, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others call it ironic antithesis or opposite-sense metaphor. Al-Qurṭubī compares the ironic 'forbearing, right-minded' in 11:87; al-Itqān compares opposite-sense glad tidings and similar taunts, while al-Sāmarrāʾī cites 'glad tidings' of punishment in 4:138. Al-Burhān and al-Sāmarrāʾī say the surrounding punishment disambiguates praise as condemnation. Al-Biqāʿī points to the sinner's present ruin; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the mockery adds to punishment."}, {"id": "44:49/q07/p3", "position": "He really had worldly standing among his people or family, but it cannot help him now.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĪsā, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Māwardī as cited by Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Ālūsī give this reading. Al-Rāzī adds that he relied on power apart from God and is made to see its failure. Bursevī includes the person's standing among his people alongside self-estimation."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q08", "question": "Whom does the address target?", "turns_on": "Whether the Abu Jahl occasion limits the address or exemplifies a wider class.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q08/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl is the specific addressee or occasion.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Qatāda, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Dāmghānī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Burhān, al-Durr, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and the Study Quran identify him. Al-Burhān cites this as specific address meant for its specific addressee. His Quraysh leadership and boasts identify him in the reports."}, {"id": "44:49/q08/p2", "position": "The address applies to the punished disbeliever or every sinner who makes the same claim.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī expressly extends it beyond Abū Jahl to every such sinner at the Resurrection. Bursevī says the verse threatens Abu Jahl and his likes; Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Iṣlāḥī and the Study Quran describe sinners, disbelievers or Hell's inhabitants more generally."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q09", "question": "What was reported to have happened with Abū Jahl and this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the occasion and timing of the boast: a worldly boast or prophetic warning before Badr, a naming episode before the Zaqqum verses, or a claim after the order to drag him into Hell.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q09/p1", "position": "He boasted that none in Mecca's valley or between its two mountains was mightier or nobler; the verse answered his claim.", "reasons": "Muqātil says he called himself Quraysh's mightiest and noblest; Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās and many exegetes vary the boast as the strongest, most honored, generous, or most protected in the valley. Al-Thaʿlabī says the phrase sharply affirms his own claim in derision. Al-Durr reports Qatāda's question of how Muḥammad could threaten such a man."}, {"id": "44:49/q09/p2", "position": "After the Prophet warned him, Abū Jahl claimed neither the Prophet nor God could harm him; he was killed and humbled at Badr, and the verse recalled his words.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Kalbī via al-Wāḥidī connect the warning with 75:34; al-Qurṭubī reports the Prophet commanded to say 'woe to you'; Ibn Kathīr cites 75:34–35. Al-Rāzī and Bursevī transmit the additional denial that the Prophet or his Lord could do anything to him. Bursevī remarks on the confused simultaneous oath by God and denial of divine power."}, {"id": "44:49/q09/p3", "position": "He called himself 'the mighty, the noble' as his name; the Zaqqum verses then descended.", "reasons": "Al-Durr gives an unnamed short report. Al-Ālūsī adds a scene where Abū Jahl asked Quraysh to guess his name, rejected ʿUmar, al-Jallās and Abū al-Ḥakam, then supplied the two titles."}, {"id": "44:49/q09/p4", "position": "After the command to drag him into Hell, he claimed unmatched might and nobility, and God replied with this taunt.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this timing from Qatāda."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q10", "question": "What does the taunt teach about power, disbelief and punishment?", "turns_on": "The explanations emphasize failed worldly strength, resurrection denial, just reversal, or an inward account of pain formerly hidden by heedlessness.", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q10/p1", "position": "Worldly power, self-exaltation and supposed invulnerability collapse under God's punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the sinner trusted power apart from God and must see what became of him. Al-Biqāʿī contrasts the boast with the warnings he den

The Study Quran notes parallel chastisements for denial in 32:20, 34:42, 52:13–16 and 83:17; on the fatḥa reading it links doubt causally to haughtiness."}, {"id": "44:49/q10/p3", "position": "The scene displays just recompense and the reversal of the sinner's former condition.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the passage uses intellectual and historical evidence for reward and punishment and depicts different fates for believers and disbelievers with complete justice. Al-Qāshānī reads a corrupted primordial nature as reversing bodily pleasure, might and psychic dignity into spiritual pain, humiliation and abasement."}, {"id": "44:49/q10/p4", "position": "Worldly heedlessness prevented him from sensing pain already caused by his injustice.", "reasons": "Bursevī says death removes the veil and reveals punishment that was present but unfelt in life."}]}
{"id": "44:49/q11", "question": "How does this scene connect with the surrounding account of judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "44:49/q11/p1", "position": "It follows arguments for judgment and depicts the disbelievers' fate alongside the believers' different fate.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the section first gives intellectual and natural arguments for reward and punishment, identifies Quraysh's denial of the afterlife as the root of rebellion, then portrays each group's fate under complete justice. {"id": "47:16/q01", "question": "To whom does 'among them' refer?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun is fixed by the immediate preceding description, by the earlier Meccan reference, or by the conduct of the hypocrites.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q01/p1", "position": "The hypocrites, especially those present with the Prophet; some accounts name particular members.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Rifaʿa ibn Zayd, al-Harith ibn Amr, and a Banu Zuhra ally. Mawardi and Qurtubi give a different five-name list including Ibn Ubayy, Rifaʿa ibn al-Tabut, Zayd ibn al-Sulayt/Salt, al-Harith, and Malik ibn al-Dakhsham/Dukhshum. Tabarsi includes hypocrites among disbelievers. Asad extends the description to later people who feign reverence while refusing Quranic meaning."}, {"id": "47:16/q01/p2", "position": "They are the previously mentioned disbelievers or unbelievers.", "reasons": "Tabarsi says hypocrites are included as disbelievers. Tabatabai takes the pronoun as unbelievers hearing recitation and instruction."}, {"id": "47:16/q01/p3", "position": "They may be people in general.", "reasons": "Razi compares Quran 2:8, where some people are mentioned after disbelievers."}, {"id": "47:16/q01/p4", "position": "They may be the people of Mecca who expelled Muhammad.", "reasons": "Razi points to 47:13."}, {"id": "47:16/q01/p5", "position": "They may be some of the people destined for Hell in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Razi points to 47:15; Biqai likewise relates them to the people of Hell before the Garden parable."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q02", "question": "What kind of listening is described?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion is a Friday sermon or general attendance, and whether the outward attention is absent, hostile, or earnest.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q02/p1", "position": "They attend the Prophet's Friday sermon, particularly when he censures hypocrites.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Farra, Zajjaj, al-Kalbi, and others connect it with the sermon and departure from the mosque; Muqatil supplies named listeners. Qushayri says exposure made hypocrites dislike revelation."}, {"id": "47:16/q02/p2", "position": "They hear the Prophet's speech or recitation in his gathering, but fail to attend to or retain it.", "reasons": "Tabari compares 6:25; believers in Ibn Jurayj's account retain what hypocrites do not. Tabatabai includes recitation and explanation of principles and laws. Islahi distinguishes aversion from feigned attendance."}, {"id": "47:16/q02/p3", "position": "Some listen intently to find a flaw in the recitation and sow doubt.", "reasons": "Biqai says the effort is hostile; his grammar note treats singular listening as few and plural turning away as many."}, {"id": "47:16/q02/p4", "position": "The listening and request may appear diligent and aimed at understanding.", "reasons": "Razi reads the sequence linked by hatta as intense listening followed by a request to repeat the speech."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q03", "question": "How does singular 'listens' agree with plural 'leave' and 'follow'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q03/p1", "position": "Man takes singular agreement by its form and plural agreement by its meaning.", "reasons": "Majaz says min is plural in sense. {"id": "47:16/q04", "question": "What does 'until' contribute to the sequence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q04/p1", "position": "It makes leaving and asking a limit or part of the listening sequence.", "reasons": "Razi says hatta, unlike wa, cannot connect unrelated clauses; this supports his reading of sustained listening and a request for repetition."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q05", "question": "What does 'they left your presence' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q05/p1", "position": "They left or parted from the Prophet's presence or gathering.", "reasons": "Mawardi identifies 'your' as the Messenger; Baghawi and Qurtubi gloss the departure, sometimes specifically from the mosque after a sermon."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q06", "question": "Who are 'those given knowledge'?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural designates learned Companions collectively or particular Companions named in reports.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q06/p1", "position": "The knowledgeable Companions or believers who understood and retained the Prophet's message.", "reasons": "Muqatil says guided by the Quran; Tabarsi says God gave knowledge and understanding; Alusi specifies attentive Companions. {"id": "47:16/q07", "question": "Why is knowledge expressed as something 'given'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q07/p1", "position": "The passive wording magnifies beneficial knowledge as God's gift.", "reasons": "Biqai says God prepares its recipients with clear minds, freedom from ego, and responsiveness to primordial nature."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q08", "question": "To whom does 'he' in their question refer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q08/p1", "position": "It refers to the Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Tabatabai identifies the pronoun explicitly; the accounts all place the inquiry after his words."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q09", "question": "Why did they ask what he had said?", "turns_on": "Whether the question signals mockery and contempt, real failure of comprehension, a pretense of obedience, or earnest request.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q09/p1", "position": "They asked mockingly, feigning ignorance or inattention and belittling the Prophet.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says the pose showed that they had paid no attention; Razi compares a clever person's sarcastic request to a dull speaker and cites 2:14. {"id": "47:16/q10", "question": "What does 'ānifan' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the root's 'beginning' denotes the near past, the present moment, or the start of the speech.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q10/p1", "position": "Just now, a short time before the present, from the sense of a beginning or foremost part.", "reasons": "Zajjaj cites newly begun pasture; Abu Zayd cites beginning speech. Wahidi cites first cold or rain and Imru al-Qays's horse run. Farisi and Wahidi cite the freshest first food in bowls. Qurtubi cites new pasture, unused cup, journey, and the nose as the first part. Bursevi and Alusi explain the nose metaphor. Qamus resolves the time as immediately before the present, not the present hour."}, {"id": "47:16/q10/p2", "position": "It means from the beginning of the Prophet's speech.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this because asking for repetition from the start would ensure they miss nothing; Mawardi also reports beginning as a sense."}, {"id": "47:16/q10/p3", "position": "It can mean at this very moment or hour.", "reasons": "Nasafi glosses it 'at this moment'; Alusi reports this alongside near past; Tabatabai allows both."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q11", "question": "What derivation and form explain 'ānifan'?", "turns_on": "Whether the attested derivation directly supports the form, or analogy and poetic forms are needed.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q11/p1", "position": "It is a participial form associated with beginning, although the simple verb is unattested.", "reasons": "Abu Ali says active participles can be formed where corresponding simple verbs are unused, comparing faqir and shadid; Ibn Atiyya applies this to both readings. Alusi calls it irregular or formed after dropping a derived prefix; Abu Hayyan derives the sense from iʾtanafa."}, {"id": "47:16/q11/p2", "position": "The root's other poetic senses include proud people and first, finest food; only the latter supports beginning here.", "reasons": "Sukkari and Abu Zayd cite al-anf for nobles refusing humiliation, and Farisi says that is not the verse's sense; a Sibawayh line on nimr supports a plural pattern. Farisi and Wahidi cite anf al-qisaʿ for freshest food. Tabarsi cites muʾtanafan for a newly begun month with 'month' omitted and al-anf al-nusur as plural evidence."}, {"id": "47:16/q11/p3", "position": "The short form can be understood by analogy with pairs such as hadhir/hadhir.", "reasons": "Farisi and Abu Ali propose the analogy, although Farisi prefers the long form because the short root meaning 'beginning' is unattested."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q12", "question": "How is the word 'ānifan' read?", "turns_on": "Whether the short Ibn Kathir transmission is sound and how its form relates to the established long reading.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q12/p1", "position": "The majority lengthen the initial vowel, reading ānifan on the fāʿil pattern.", "reasons": "Farisi says all readers other than the reported Ibn Kathir variant use it; Tabarsi calls it famous. Farisi prefers it because the verse means newly begun from iʾtanafa; Wahidi upholds the common reading and calls al-Bazzi's short report a mistaken supposition."}, {"id": "47:16/q12/p2", "position": "A transmission of Ibn Kathir reads the initial vowel short, anifan on the faʿl pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Bazzi transmits it while Qunbul also reports long; Ibn al-Jawzi adds Ikrima, Humayd, and Ibn Muhaysin. Zamakhshari says the form is accusative; Farisi and Abu Ali explain it by analogy to hadhir/hadhir, but Wahidi rejects this attribution."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q13", "question": "What is the syntactic role of 'ānifan'?", "turns_on": "Whether the temporal gloss establishes grammatical adverb status or only conveys the sense of a circumstantial participle.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q13/p1", "position": "It is an adverbial accusative of time, meaning just now.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari gives this parse; Baydawi allows it, and Tabatabai adopts it. Abu Hayyan, the Sheikh cited by Samin, and Biqai reject the parse because grammarians do not classify it as an adverb."}, {"id": "47:16/q13/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative referring to the speaker, what he had just begun to say.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa supplies the expansion mādhā qāla muʾtanafan; Abu Hayyan applies it to the statement begun before they left. {"id": "47:16/q14", "question": "What does God's sealing of their hearts signify?", "turns_on": "Whether the seal is a divine mark, figurative condition, abandonment to choice, or consequence of their own conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q14/p1", "position": "Their hearts are marked or closed so they cannot believe or understand for benefit.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies disbelief and failure to grasp faith. Biqai adds rigid indifference; Ibn Kathir adds lack of sound understanding and intention. Study Quran notes outward profession with inward blindness. Jishumi equates tabʿ and khatm as marking; Raghib says tabʿ shapes or imprints, broader than sealing but narrower than engraving."}, {"id": "47:16/q14/p2", "position": "The seal may be understood literally or metaphorically.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya refers back to his earlier discussion without choosing between them."}, {"id": "47:16/q14/p3", "position": "The hearts may bear a stamp of disbelief or be left to the people's own choice.", "reasons": "Tabarsi reports both explanations."}, {"id": "47:16/q14/p4", "position": "Sealing means loss of perfected knowledge, paired with following desires as loss of righteous action.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the two clauses can also be read with the second explanatory of the first."}, {"id": "47:16/q14/p5", "position": "The seal expresses an incapacity to receive revelation after persistent wrongdoing or desire.", "reasons": "Bursevi says they no longer turn toward good; Elmalili says desire prevents the Prophet's words entering comprehension; Islahi says misdeeds extinguish innate vision; Kuranyolu says the conduct conditions mind and heart."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q15", "question": "How are sealing and following desires related?", "turns_on": "Whether desire causes the seal, the seal helps explain desire, or the two clauses describe distinct intellectual and practical losses.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q15/p1", "position": "Their following desires brings about or explains the sealed heart.", "reasons": "Asad explicitly makes sealing result from following desires, citing 2:7; Elmalili and Islahi likewise link desire or misdeeds to loss of receptivity. Tabatabai calls the second clause explanatory of the first and contrasts those pure in original nature."}, {"id": "47:16/q15/p2", "position": "Sealing leaves them without faith and understanding, and they follow desires instead of truth.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the seal is disbelief and desires are disbelief and hypocrisy. Ibn Kathir pairs defective understanding and intention. Baydawi says the two conditions explain mockery. Razi says they turned away because they could not understand or would not listen for benefit."}, {"id": "47:16/q15/p3", "position": "The pair describes loss of knowledge and loss of righteous action.", "reasons": "Tabatabai offers this reading while allowing the explanatory relation too."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q16", "question": "What are 'desires' and what does following them entail?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is confined to a reported occasion or extends by its general wording.", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q16/p1", "position": "Ahywāʾ is the plural of hawā, the soul's inclination or desire; following it opposes proof and truth.", "reasons": "Jishumi distinguishes al-hawā, air, and istahwā, calling toward desire; Tabarsi also gives the plural and verb. Biqai says it abandons reason, restraint, and the great discourse for worldly accumulation. Alusi says they turn to what has no good; Bursevi says false desires explain fruitless conduct."}, {"id": "47:16/q16/p2", "position": "The desires are disbelief and hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Muqatil explicitly gives both; Baghawi says disbelief, and Wahidi transmits Muqatil."}, {"id": "47:16/q16/p3", "position": "The warning applies generally to every unbeliever and innovator.", "reasons": "Jishumi says wording extends beyond the occasion and rejects confinement to Abu Jahl and associates."}, {"id": "47:16/q16/p4", "position": "It refers specifically to Abu Jahl and his polytheist associates.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this occasion but objects that the wording is general."}]}

{"id": "47:16/q18", "question": "How does the verse connect to nearby passages and the surah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q18/p1", "position": "It continues the treatment of diseased hearts, hypocrisy, and the relation of deeds to belief.", "reasons": "Tabatabai includes apostates after faith; Islahi says 16–19 turn to the hidden enemy and 16–38 expose weakness and collusion before a major campaign. {"id": "47:16/q19", "question": "What inward contrast does the verse suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q19/p1", "position": "The polished heart witnesses truth, whereas the lower self makes innovation and disobedience attractive and follows desire.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the first gains insight and the second strays from God and Paradise."}]}
{"id": "47:16/q20", "question": "What does the cited lexical digression say 'sky' can mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:16/q20/p1", "position": "Samāʾ names what is elevated and can denote the visible sky, clouds, rain, a roof, or the ceiling of Paradise or Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi derives it from sumūw, cites samā for rising sight or a visible figure and samāwa for the moon's body, and illustrates the senses with 2:29, 64:3, 51:22, 51:47, 15:22, 71:11, 22:15, and 11:107–108. {"id": "47:17/q01", "question": "Who are those who have been guided?", "turns_on": "Whether the description refers generally to believers or specifically to earlier scriptural believers who accepted Muhammad.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q01/p1", "position": "The believers or Muslims who receive the truth and follow it.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi (Wahidi), the majority (Ibn al-Jawzi), and others identify them as Muslims or believers. Nahhas stresses acceptance and action; Biqai describes sincere faith, surrender, listening, and spiritual effort; Razi and Kuranyolu stress understanding and acting on what is heard; Tabatabai calls it following sound innate nature and truth. Ibn Kathir says they seek guidance and remain firm; Ibn Atiyya says the wording credits their effort. Jishumi contrasts heedless and mindful listeners through Qatada's report."}, {"id": "47:17/q01/p2", "position": "People of Scripture who followed their earlier prophets and then believed in Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya's group specifies Christians guided by belief in Jesus before accepting Muhammad. {"id": "47:17/q02", "question": "Who or what increases their guidance?", "turns_on": "The implicit subject of زادهم and whether the preceding speech, revelation, or hypocritical conduct functions as its cause.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q02/p1", "position": "God increases it, through His grace, inspiration, proofs, or revelation.", "reasons": "Zajjaj prefers God as the pronoun's referent. Ibn Atiyya lists understanding, evidence, laws, prohibitions, and reports as means; Abu Hayyan points to God's sealing in the preceding verse and His giving in the next clause. Razi also pairs God's increase with His sealing of hypocritical hearts. Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas and Muqatil on God granting the increase; Baydawi and Alusi mention enabling grace and inspiration. Islahi links the increase to preserving innate light and cites 9:124–125."}, {"id": "47:17/q02/p2", "position": "The Qur'an or its recitation increases it.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj names the Qur'an; Wahidi's Dahhak says believers rejoice at each revelation; Qurtubi says the heard Qur'an multiplies certainty. Tabrisi explicitly offers Qur'an recitation as the implicit agent; Razi includes God's words among what they heard."}, {"id": "47:17/q02/p3", "position": "The Messenger or his words increase it.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says what the Messenger said; Wahidi links it to his immediately preceding words. Razi contrasts the believers' understanding of the Prophet's and God's words with the hypocrites' failure in 47:16. Ibn Atiyya's special reading makes Muhammad the cause of further guidance for Christians. Alusi calls a proposed prophetic subject contrary to the apparent sense and argues for alignment with God's sealing of hearts."}, {"id": "47:17/q02/p4", "position": "The hypocrites' mockery, words, or turning away increase it by provoking believers' insight.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and Zajjaj identify mockery or turning away. Ibn Atiyya says believers marvel at the hypocrites' confusion, thank God for faith, and gain insight, with the cause expressed as agent. Razi says they abhor and avoid that conduct; Abu Hayyan says they praise God and strengthen their support of religion. Alusi calls this suggestion very remote and scarcely worth considering."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q03", "question": "What is the increase in guidance?", "turns_on": "Whether added guidance is chiefly understanding, greater faith, new revelation and rulings, sustained practice, or the capacity to guide others.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q03/p1", "position": "New understanding, knowledge, insight, and evidence.", "reasons": "Nahhas includes revealed verses, proofs, signs, and arguments. Al-Rabi calls it added knowledge; Dahhak says they understand what they hear and act on it; al-Kalbi adds religious insight and affirmation of the Prophet. Ibn Atiyya mentions growing knowledge and belief from laws and reports. Ibn al-Jawzi reports knowledge or insight; Razi cites following the best of what is heard (39:17–18) and affirming ambiguous revelation (3:7). Abu Hayyan mentions understanding and proofs; Tabatabai says the increase perfects knowledge. Study Quran reports faith, knowledge, and insight."}, {"id": "47:17/q03/p2", "position": "Further faith, certainty, conviction, or openness of heart.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi say God opens hearts further to existing faith. Qurtubi says hearing the Qur'an multiplies certainty. Ibn Atiyya says their knowledge and belief grow; Nasafi allows an opening of hearts. Tabatabai says faith and guidance have degrees. Razi contrasts this with sealed hypocritical hearts; Islahi links it to preserved innate light."}, {"id": "47:17/q03/p3", "position": "Knowledge and obedience to successive abrogating rulings.", "reasons": "Muqatil says decisive verses abrogated an earlier command. Abu Salih says an abrogator itself may be the additional guidance; Muqatil ibn Hayyan adds reward for obedience to the earlier command before following the new one. Atiyya names knowledge of abrogating and abrogated rulings; Ibn Abbas says the Qur'an guided first, then such knowledge increased guidance."}, {"id": "47:17/q03/p4", "position": "Deeper practice, steadfastness, and guidance toward truth.", "reasons": "Mawardi says truth leads to further truth. Dahhak joins understanding to acting. Qushayri says recognition without dispute yields steadfastness on truth's paths. Ibn Kathir says seekers find guidance and remain firm. Kuranyolu connects sound reasoning and the Prophet's explanations to continuing obedience; Islahi says God nurtures virtue according to capacity and desire. Razi invokes 6:90 as a command to follow earlier people's guidance and identifies hudā as the verbal noun of هدَى; Biqai links 10:9 to God's guidance of believers by their faith."}, {"id": "47:17/q03/p5", "position": "A move from being guided listeners to guides who explain the Qur'an with proof.", "reasons": "Razi proposes that listeners understand and teach others; they guard against unsupported or merely personal interpretation."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q04", "question": "How is وَٱلَّذِينَ ٱهْتَدَوْا۟ parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative expression starts as a nominative subject or depends on an implied verb.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q04/p1", "position": "It is nominative as the sentence's subject.", "reasons": "Samin gives this parsing; Alusi calls it the apparent reading."}, {"id": "47:17/q04/p2", "position": "It is accusative by preoccupation, governed by an omitted verb explained by the following verb.", "reasons": "Both Samin and Alusi allow this construction."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q05", "question": "How is هُدًۭى construed and why is it indefinite?", "turns_on": "Whether hudan fills a second object slot or specifies the increase.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q05/p1", "position": "It is the second object of زاد, with indefiniteness magnifying the added guidance.", "reasons": "Alusi calls this the more apparent construction and says the indefinite form magnifies the gift."}, {"id": "47:17/q05/p2", "position": "It is a specification of the increase; its indefiniteness magnifies it.", "reasons": "Alusi records this alternative while still explaining the indefinite form as magnifying the increase."}]}

{"id": "47:17/q08", "question": "How is تَقْوَىٰهُمْ grammatically formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q08/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun annexed to its subject, those who are guided.", "reasons": "Samin gives this analysis; Abu Hayyan uses it when explaining that God made them God-fearing."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q09", "question": "How was وَءَاتَىٰهُمْ read differently?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q09/p1", "position": "A variant reads 'and bestowed/gave them' in place of آتاهم.", "reasons": "Tha'labi attributes a bestowed/gave wording to Ibn Masud and al-A'mash. Ibn Atiyya gives al-A'mash's وأنطاهم, equates it with أعطاهم, and notes Muhammad ibn Talha's transmission from his father and its occurrence in Abd Allah's codex. Qurtubi reports أعطاهم."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q10", "question": "How do inward readings describe growth in guidance and piety?", "turns_on": "Which stage or practice the spiritual reading takes as the verse's increase.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q10/p1", "position": "Sincere seekers reach guidance's station and grow by reaching the Guide.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata gives this account, transmitted by Sulami and Bursevi."}, {"id": "47:17/q10/p2", "position": "Reflection and spiritual striving deepen into disclosure, witnessing, and certainty.", "reasons": "Qushayri says striving gains lights of witnessing, reflection on proof gains the spirit of disclosure, and knowledge of certainty is followed by truth of certainty. Biqai describes illuminated hearts as vessels of wisdom. Qushayri adds that the manners of intimate prayer lead to salvation and elevated ranks."}, {"id": "47:17/q10/p3", "position": "Taqwa is turning to God and healing desire by leaving worldly craving.", "reasons": "Al-Tibi calls following desire a spiritual illness, abiding by taqwa divine medicine, and cites 26:80; he also interprets perfected taqwa as turning wholly to God and cites 3:102."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q11", "question": "How does the verse contrast the surrounding account of hypocrites?", "turns_on": "Whether the relevant link is the immediate contrast with hypocrites or the move onward to the Hour.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q11/p1", "position": "It contrasts receptive believers with hypocrites who hear without benefit and follow desire.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya points to 47:16 and says the contrast credits believers' effort. Jishumi says the earlier hearers were hypocrites who did not seek guidance; Qatada contrasts heedless and mindful listeners. Razi says the believers' understanding removes any claim that revelation is obscure: the hypocrites' failure is blindness of heart. Al-Tibi pairs the guided with desire-followers and increased guidance with sealed hearts, though Alusi says this pattern is not decisive. Tabatabai says guidance counters sealed-heart misguidance and taqwa counters desire: increased guidance perfects knowledge and taqwa perfects action, while sealing and desire remove those perfections; he allows the second clause to explain the first. Islahi calls hypocrites the Muslims' hidden enemy whose hypocrisy grows from the same hearing that strengthens believers. Tabatabai situates the passage after diseased hearts and apostasy."}, {"id": "47:17/q11/p2", "position": "The contrast leads onward to a warning that the Hour is near.", "reasons": "Wahidi says the commentary then warns Meccan disbelievers that nothing from them will be accepted when the Hour comes; Elmali says believers' increased guidance and taqwa prepare them to meet God at the appointed hour."}]}
{"id": "47:17/q12", "question": "How is God's increase of guidance and gift of taqwa related to human action?", "turns_on": "Whether divine help creates faith or piety directly, gives an effective capacity, or facilitates a person's own response.", "positions": [{"id": "47:17/q12/p1", "position": "Guidance's increase is divine facilitating grace, while people themselves accept, reflect, and act.", "reasons": "Jishumi rejects the Mujabbira's claim that the increase means God creates faith and instead calls it لطف. Ibn Atiyya emphasizes believers' own effort in seeking guidance; Islahi says God nurtures virtue according to retained innate capacity and desire."}, {"id": "47:17/q12/p2", "position": "God creates piety in people, as Ash'aris say of human acts.", "reasons": "Alusi explicitly gives the Ash'ari account and says making them God-fearing fits it; Bursevi also says God creates piety. Jishumi rejects analogous creation of faith as the meaning of increased guidance."}, {"id": "47:17/q12/p3", "position": "God creates an effective capacity by His permission through which they practice piety.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this account to al-Kurani's presentation of al-Ash'ari and other investigators and says making them God-fearing accommodates it."}]}
{"id": "49:13/q01", "question": "Who is addressed as people?", "turns_on": "How far the universal opening extends into the genealogical description.", "positions": [{"id": "49:13/q01/p1", "position": "All humanity, believers and others.", "reasons": "Al-Damghānī gives the general sense; al-Biqāʿī explicitly includes unbelievers."}, {"id": "49:13/q01/p2", "position": "The opening is general, but the following tribal detail specifically concerns Arabs.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās distinguishes address from genealogy; ʿUmar calls the verse addressed to Arabs."}]}
